scenes.title: The beds exist; the coordination does not
scenes.narration: You cannot build your way out of this, because the beds already exist. They are lost to callbacks that run for hours, to cubicles that can only accept one kind of patient, and to discharges that clear in the afternoon when the queue formed throughout the night.

scenes.title: The decision, synthesised — then dispatched without a call
scenes.narration: The first fix is the decision itself. Today a doctor writes notes, pages a specialist, then waits for a callback. Instead, vitals and lab results are read on arrival and become a proposed acuity tier, admitting specialty and level of monitoring — reviewed, not retyped. And where two doctors disagree, we take the higher tier and combine both monitoring orders, because averaging two clinical opinions is the one thing a system must never do. From there the admission reaches bed management as data.

scenes.title: Not every admission needs a scarce acute bed
scenes.narration: The second fix is admitting fewer people at all. Diversion was always possible — it was just buried under enough paperwork that clinicians took the acute bed instead. So the alternatives became the easy path: a patient stable enough gets hospital-level monitoring at home with a daily visit, and a patient who mainly needs weeks of rehabilitation goes to a community hospital as a digital referral, with a thirty-minute clock on the reply.

scenes.title: The insight that recovers ghost capacity is the ordering
scenes.narration: The third fix recovers those five frozen beds, and it comes down to ordering. Fill the part-used cubicles first, with patients who already match the people in them. Only then open a clean cubicle — and open it for a whole group at once. And when a single patient is the only reason a room is unusable, move that patient, not the room. Same beds, same safety rules, a different order of operations.

scenes.title: 07a-bed-lifecycle-capture
scenes.narration: First the board itself. Every bed in the hospital is in exactly one of four states — being cleaned, ready, promised to someone, or occupied — and the colours are simply how a coordinator reads a whole level at a glance. Every decision that follows is a move between those four, which is why a bed can never quietly go missing.

scenes.title: 08a-solver-recommendation-capture
scenes.narration: Mr Tan Ah Meng again — the request we watched arrive without a call. He needs heart monitoring, and he is a falls risk. Every bed in the hospital is scored against four rules the system will never break — among them, never mixing genders in a cubicle, and never placing a patient where the monitoring is not installed — and then three softer preferences it weighs, like keeping a specialty together on one ward. Three beds come back in under fifty milliseconds, each showing why it scored where it did.

steps.target: Select button on the Tan Ah Meng row

scenes.title: 08b-batch-holding-capture
scenes.narration: Now the batching step. Three waiting patients share a ward class, a gender and an infection status — enough to fill a clean cubicle completely — so the whole room is offered as a single decision. One approval instead of three placements, and no half-used cubicle left behind to freeze later.

scenes.title: 08c-cohort-swap-capture
scenes.narration: And this is the unlock. One patient, still down in the emergency department, is the only reason an entire ward cannot be released to the group waiting for it. The system offers him an equal bed — same class, same monitoring — and one approval frees the room. He loses nothing; the ward becomes usable.

scenes.title: 08d-solver-config-capture
scenes.narration: None of that scoring is hard-coded. A coordinator can retune how much specialty grouping, cubicle packing or falls-risk proximity counts, and save it while the hospital is running. A dengue cluster changes what a good bed looks like — and that should never need a software release.

scenes.title: The anxiety removed at the front, the exit begun at the back
scenes.narration: The fourth fix sits at both ends of the stay. At the front, the family stops asking the triage nurse: they see their position among the patients in their own ward class, and an honest reason when it slips. At the back, discharge starts two or three days early, the medicines are packed overnight instead of chased at noon, and the cleaning clock starts the moment a bed empties.

scenes.title: 10b-tracker-delay-tag-capture
scenes.narration: And when the news is bad, the tone changes instead of going quiet. Mdm Wong Siew Kuan's room needs a deep clean before anyone can enter it. Her tracker says exactly that, in plain words, with a number she can call — because an explained wait is a different experience from an unexplained one, even when it is the same length.

scenes.title: 10c-discharge-runway-capture
scenes.narration: Up on the ward now. Every occupied bed carries an expected discharge date, set two to three days ahead, with how confident the nurse is and the clinical reason for it — so bed management can see a bed coming before it exists.

scenes.title: 10d-bedside-meds-capture
scenes.narration: Medicines are the single biggest delay on discharge day. So the morning sign-off does two jobs at once: it clears the patient to leave, and it queues the take-home prescription for delivery to the bedside. One button confirms it arrived, and the bed frees before eleven instead of after lunch — the difference between this queue clearing today and tomorrow.

scenes.title: 10e-housekeeping-turnover-capture
scenes.narration: And this is the last of those four handoffs — the one from the ward to housekeeping. Housekeeping runs its own thirty-minute countdown, and signing a bed off returns it to the matching engine automatically. Nobody phones bed management — the loop closes without anyone carrying the message.

scenes.title: Every decision is measured
scenes.narration: The fifth fix is the one that makes the other four accountable. Every step you have seen writes a record — twenty-one bed requests in this dataset, every one of them digital, not one placed by phone. And each figure can be produced two independent ways: a database query for the dashboards, and the audit log for alerting. A number nobody can reproduce is not a measurement.
